title: Antarctic summer extent gave no clear forecast gain after prior winter extent in 2000-2024
abstract: We tested whether Antarctic February extent adds information about September extent after the previous September extent is known. We used Sea Ice Index Version 4 daily means and 45 annual triples in 1980-2024. In 25 forecasts for 2000-2024, summer extent reduced mean squared error by 15.6% against a time trend alone. Against a model with time and prior winter extent, the reduction was -0.93%, with a conditional 95% three-year block interval of -25.0% to +17.9%. The summer coefficient fell from 0.517 to 0.267 after the prior winter control; its block interval was -0.188 to 0.621. Fixed five-year group means held 66.0% of the detrended summer-winter covariance. The annual first-difference slope was -0.004. These checks show sensitivity to timescale and forecast baseline. They do not prove that summer effects are absent or that a slow state caused the link. Few recent low years, changing climate, extent-only data and simple linear models limit inference. The package gives inputs, source hashes, code, forecasts, uncertainty, a figure and independent numerical checks.

display.caption: Antarctic summer-winter association changes with timescale removal. Adding summer extent to a forecast with prior winter extent gives no clear average error reduction in 2000-2024.

citations.reason: Its endpoint test and period sensitivity motivate our new conditional forecast test. We rebuild from raw files and do not copy code.
